analysis.one_liner: Raises criminal fines and prison terms for employers whose willful safety violations injure or kill workers.
analysis.headline: The bill, which had bipartisan sponsorship and a Senate hearing, was never voted on and died in committee when the 102nd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it a serious crime for an employer to willfully violate federal workplace safety rules. If a willful violation seriously injures a worker, executives could face up to five years in prison, and if it kills a worker, up to ten years for a repeat offense — penalties that today top out around six months to a year behind bars and small fixed fines. It would also bar companies from paying their executives' fines for them, and make clear that states can prosecute workplace deaths and injuries under their own criminal laws.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers in dangerous industries. The people most at risk from willful safety violations — miners, construction and factory workers, meatpackers — would gain a real deterrent: employers and executives who knowingly ignore safety rules could face prison and large fines instead of minor penalties treated as a cost of doing business. Co-workers and families of injured workers would also gain, because states could bring their own criminal charges when a worker is seriously hurt or killed on the job.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the maximum prison term for a willful OSHA violation that kills a worker from one year to ten years, and raises the maximum for a willful violation causing serious bodily injury from six months to five years (ten years for repeat offenders) [S3].
Replaces fixed dollar caps on criminal fines with the open-ended federal fine schedule used for other serious crimes, so penalties can scale with the size and gravity of the offense [S3].

Makes it a new crime to willfully violate a safety standard in a way that causes serious bodily injury short of death — filling a gap, since current law only sets higher penalties when a violation results in death [S3].
Bars companies from paying criminal fines imposed on their directors, officers, or agents, so the individuals responsible bear the penalty personally [S3].
Clarifies that state and local prosecutors can pursue criminal cases under state law, closing off a federal preemption argument for employers [S3].
Defines 'serious bodily injury' to include a substantial risk of death, prolonged unconsciousness, lasting disfigurement, or lasting loss of a bodily or mental function [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers in hazardous industries and their executives. Companies would face much larger fines, and individual directors and officers could face prison time — with the bill written so the company cannot reimburse them. Businesses that currently treat the small OSHA criminal penalties (fines as low as $1,000 to $20,000 and at most a year in prison) as an absorbable cost would lose that shield [S3].

drawbacks.text: Criminal liability for 'willful' violations that cause serious injury would expose individual managers to up to 5 or 10 years in prison, and businesses argue this could push risk-averse behavior, harder-fought enforcement cases, and higher compliance costs that get passed on [S3].

The bill raises penalties sharply without adding new enforcement resources for OSHA's inspection force, so the tougher penalties only matter in the cases inspectors and prosecutors actually bring [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers, the benefit is a genuine deterrent: today a willful safety violation that kills a worker carries at most a year in prison and a modest fine, which critics long argued makes fatalities a calculable business cost. The costs fall on employers and executives, and the main good-faith objection — that criminal exposure for managers may raise compliance costs — is the point of the bill. The design is straightforward: it raises penalties and keeps state prosecutions available. The main design weakness is that it does not fund more inspections, so the new penalties apply only where violations are actually caught and prosecuted.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee, got a subcommittee hearing a week later, and then was never brought up for a committee vote or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Metzenbaum and seven other senators, including one Republican, introduced the bill on February 20, 1991, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources [S1][S3].
The Labor subcommittee held hearings on the bill on February 28, 1991, printing them as S.Hrg. 102-87 [S5].

After the hearing, no further action was taken: the full committee never voted on the bill and the Senate never considered it, and it expired when the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers and their executives are better off: the existing modest criminal penalties for willful workplace safety violations — fines of $1,000 to $20,000 and prison terms of six months to a year — remained unchanged for the whole Congress [S3].

for.name: Sen. Howard Metzenbaum
for.role: U.S. Senator (D-OH), sponsor; chaired the Labor Subcommittee that held the bill's hearing
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and, through his Labor subcommittee, held a hearing on it eight days after introduction [S1][S5].

for.name: Sen. Jeffords, Adams, Simon, Mikulski, Harkin, Kennedy, and Dodd
for.role: Original cosponsors (7 senators, including the Labor and Human Resources Committee chairman)

for.name: 1 Senate Republican
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, giving it bipartisan sponsorship from the start [S4].

against.name: Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources
against.what_they_did: Took no action after the subcommittee hearing: never ordered the bill reported and never sent it to the Senate floor for a vote [S5].

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsors were bipartisan — eight senators including one Republican — and no opposition vote or statement appears in the record; it simply died in committee without a vote [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Employers in hazardous industries (construction, manufacturing, mining, meatpacking)
industries.note: The bill would have exposed these companies to unlimited federal fines and prison terms for willful safety violations, replacing fixed fines of $1,000–$20,000 and at most a year in prison. Its defeat preserved the status quo in which criminal penalties for worker deaths and serious injuries remain small relative to the profits at stake [S3].

Executives could have faced 5–10 years in prison for willful violations causing serious injury or death, and the bill expressly barred companies from paying their personal fines. Defeat of the bill preserved the existing regime of minimal personal criminal exposure for workplace safety failures [S3].
